title: Network hop & streaming latency deep dive - Zenith Retail
summary: Detailed technical deep dive focused on p95/p99 tail latency causes across network hops, streaming vs non-streaming APIs, KV cache behavior and batching tradeoffs. Agreed to run a controlled lab with Zenith tokenized prompts, measure cold vs warm cache, and validate streaming improvements over HTTP/2 gRPC in their VPC environment.
topics: network hops, MTU and TLS handshake impact
KV cache (prefix vs full) and warm/cold effects
quantization impact on throughput and latencies
VPC/on-prem networking considerations and firewall rules

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-05-21 15:00 PDT | Duration 58m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Emily (Redwood SE), Jordan (Infra Eng) -- Alex (Zenith), Priya (Zenith SRE), Marcus (Platform), Sofia (PM)

00:00 Samir (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick agenda: dig into p95/p99 tail causes, figure out what network hops vs runtime are contributing, and agree next steps.
00:18 Alex (Zenith): Yeah thanks, high priority for us. We're seeing occasional spikes, usually during heavy end-of-day flushes, p99 is like 1.4s while p95 is around 220-260ms, and it feels random.
00:34 Priya (Zenith): To add, we have an HTTP proxy inside the VPC that terminates TLS and then forwards to our autoscaling pool. Not sure if that adds jitter.
00:48 Emily (Redwood): Ok, good color. We'll try to separate network-induced latency from model runtime. A typical approach is instrument per-hop timing and also instrument internal runtime phases: tokenize, KV cache lookup, attention pass, kernel enqueue.
01:10 Marcus (Zenith): Quick Q: is streaming really lower tail vs non-streaming or are we just seeing different jitter profiles?
01:22 Jordan (Redwood): Streaming often reduces tail because you can emit tokens as soon as they're available; non-streaming waits for full generation which accumulates variance. But if there is network buffering or proxies that coalesce, streaming can actually be hurt.
01:48 Samir (Redwood): Right, and we saw cases where a reverse proxy had a default 64KB buffer, so the first bytes would wait until buffer fills or flush policy triggers. That turned out to add 200-300ms intermittently.
02:10 Alex (Zenith): Ah that explains some of it. Our infra team mentioned a managed proxy, we didn't think about chunking policies.
02:22 Priya (Zenith): Also curious about KV cache. When you say warm vs cold, how big is the delta typically?
02:32 Emily (Redwood): Good question. In our infra, warm KV cache hits avoid recomputing prefix attention states; for long conversations the delta can be 40-70% token latency improvement on per-token time in the steady-state. But the cold-to-warm transition can spike because of cache population and backend fetches.
02:58 Alex (Zenith): So cold first request to a shard could be higher by... like 300-800ms?
03:08 Emily (Redwood): In some configs, yes. Depends on model size and KV store locality. If KV lives on the same GPU host, it's microseconds to low ms; if it requires an RPC to another host due to sharding, that's tens to hundreds of ms.
03:28 Marcus (Zenith): We're running a pinned dedicated pool but with occasional cross-node fetches due to shard rebalancing.
03:38 Jordan (Redwood): Rebalancing can be a silent tail killer. We recommend sticky routing for active sessions or consistent hashing with failover that prefetches adjacent KV partitions.
03:58 Samir (Redwood): Also quantization — if you push to int8 or newer 4-bit schedules, throughput improves but you sometimes see slightly higher variance due to additional kernel paths and fallback to FP when kernel misses. Not huge but measurable at p99.
04:22 Sofia (Zenith): We've been experimenting with int8 in our bench but worried about regression. How do you measure quality-vs-latency?
04:34 Emily (Redwood): We pair A/B by prompt sets and automated evals. In the lab we look for delta in generation tokens and semantic similarity scores. For production, we gate quantized models behind canary rules and monitor regressions.
04:48 Alex (Zenith): Can you walk through an example trace where p99 popped?
05:00 Emily (Redwood): Sure, here's a simplified trace from another customer: client -> VPC proxy (TLS handshake sometimes retried) -> NAT gateway -> Redwood front proxy -> routing to dedicated pool -> model shard lookup -> KV RPC to neighboring host -> kernel enqueue -> GPU execution -> stream back through same path. The long poles were NAT rebindings and KV RPCs.
05:30 Priya (Zenith): NAT rebindings — we have AWS NAT gateway behind many private subnets. That could add 100-200ms during ephemeral port exhaustion?
05:42 Jordan (Redwood): Exactly, ephemeral port reuse or flow table churn in managed NATs can add spikes. We recommend measured egress capacity and maybe using a dedicated ENI for steady flows.
05:58 Marcus (Zenith): Ok that rings true. One of our spikes lines up with our nightly export hitting the same NAT.
06:10 Samir (Redwood): Practically, Emily and Jordan will run a controlled lab. We'll capture per-hop histograms, and include streaming vs non-streaming with different buffer sizes. Also test with KV warm and cold states, and quantized vs FP kernels.
06:30 Alex (Zenith): For instrumentation, what do you need from us?
06:36 Emily (Redwood): We'll need sample prompts, VPC egress path (what proxies/NATs), and any L7 proxies in front of the Redwood endpoint. Also if you have a recording of a p99 spike that'd help.
06:52 Priya (Zenith): We'll send the topology and a list of times.
07:00 Samir (Redwood): Cool. Now let's deep dive into streaming vs non-streaming behavior — Emily?
07:06 Emily (Redwood): Streaming path uses HTTP/2 or gRPC bidi streams. It's more sensitive to per-segment backpressure. If your client or proxies have small windows, the server can send but it sits in the pipe. Non-streaming collects tokens server-side, then sends a single payload — less variance in network but higher overall latency.
07:34 Alex (Zenith): We use an API gateway that does connection pooling but it's L7 and terminates HTTP/2, then re-issues HTTP/1 to some internal endpoints. Could that be the issue?
07:46 Jordan (Redwood): That's a big red flag. Terminating HTTP/2 and converting to HTTP/1 removes end-to-end streaming benefits and introduces buffering. If the GW waits for end of response or chunk coalescing, tail suffers.
08:04 Priya (Zenith): Our vendor also does TLS offload, so the crypto cost is moved to the proxy. But you said TLS handshake retries show up. How to detect that?
08:14 Emily (Redwood): In traces we look for repeated TLS SNI renegotiations or short-lived sockets. Socket lifecycle events and TLS session resumption metrics are helpful — a cache miss for session tickets will add a full handshake time.
08:34 Alex (Zenith): We can expose those via our VPC flow logs and proxy metrics.
08:40 Samir (Redwood): Good. Now batching — if we batch small requests we save GPU time but add latency. What's the sweet spot?
08:52 Jordan (Redwood): It depends on arrival distribution. Redwood's continuous batching aims to batch within a deadline (e.g., 15ms target) then flush. If your SLO for p95 is 200ms, you can tolerate small batching delays; for p99 scenarios you must tune batching thresholds and max batch sizes.
09:10 Marcus (Zenith): Are there runtime knobs we can expose to our app?
09:14 Emily (Redwood): Yes: max_batch_size, batch_timeout_ms, and per-route priority. Also cache warm thresholds and sticky routing per session.
09:24 Alex (Zenith): About KV cache — is it local to GPU or a separate service? We've heard it as both in different docs, bit unclear.
09:34 Jordan (Redwood): It can be both. For low-latency setups we co-locate KV on the GPU host memory; for capacity-optimized setups, we shard and do RPCs. Co-located KV gives best p99s.
09:48 Priya (Zenith): If we can't co-locate due to memory, you'd recommend prefetch?
09:54 Emily (Redwood): Prefetch and proactive caching for hot sessions helps. Also consider hybrid: keep recent prefixes locally and cold prefixes in RPC store.
10:06 Samir (Redwood): Let's go through a hypothetical lab plan — we'll run 3 experiments: baseline non-streaming, streaming with small chunking, and streaming with large chunking + tunable proxy flush. Each experiment will be run with cold KV, warm KV and with int8 quantized model.
10:30 Sofia (Zenith): How many concurrent sessions should we simulate? Our production is bursty, peaks at ~400QPS during promos.
10:38 Emily (Redwood): For tail analysis, simulate 500 concurrent sessions with realistic think times. We'll inject background NAT churn and a synthetic proxy buffer to emulate your gateway.
10:52 Alex (Zenith): You mentioned earlier about kernel fallback causing variance with quantized kernels — can you expand?
10:58 Jordan (Redwood): Some kernels are optimized for certain sequence lengths or attention patterns. When a kernel isn't available (e.g., longer sequence than precompiled path) runtime falls back to a generic kernel that has different latency. Quantized paths add a conversion step sometimes. The result is more dispersion in per-token timing at p99.
11:22 Priya (Zenith): Is there a way to log kernel path selection in prod?
11:27 Emily (Redwood): Yes, we can instrument kernel selections and annotate traces. That will tell us how often fallbacks happen and correlate them to tail events.
11:36 Marcus (Zenith): On the networking side, is MTU mismatch a real problem?
11:40 Jordan (Redwood): Absolutely. If there's an MTU mismatch you can see segmentation and reassembly delays. Also path MTU discovery failures sometimes cause retransmits that look like jitter.
11:52 Alex (Zenith): We'll run an MTU sweep across route components.
11:56 Samir (Redwood): Good. A few quick notes on observability: please enable per-token telemetry for a sample set, capture p50/p95/p99 histograms, and add per-hop latencies. We'll produce a waterfall chart.
12:12 Emily (Redwood): Also instrument connection reuse stats — sockets opened per minute, TLS session resumption hit rate, and proxy queue depths.
12:24 Sofia (Zenith): Any quick wins we can try before the lab?
12:28 Jordan (Redwood): If your gateway allows it, enable HTTP/2 passthrough or preserve bidi streams to the backend — that often reduces tail. Disable proxy coalescing and increase flush/window sizes. Also make sure your NAT is provisioned for ephemeral port capacity.
12:46 Priya (Zenith): Will do.
12:50 Alex (Zenith): About the lab artifacts — what will Redwood provide?
12:54 Samir (Redwood): We'll provide CSV timelines, waterfall charts, kernel selection logs, KV hit/miss traces, config diffs for batch settings, and a short recommendations doc. We'll also include the scripts so you can re-run. Deck link: https://redwood/shared/zenith-latency-lab-2025-05-21.pdf
13:18 Emily (Redwood): One more gotcha — if you use aggressive autoscaling, cold-starting new GPU nodes can spike latencies due to cold cache. Consider warm pools or pre-warmed nodes for peak windows.
13:36 Marcus (Zenith): Our autoscaler does scale-up in 2 minutes — that's likely the nightly spike. We'll consider warm pool.
13:44 Sofia (Zenith): Ok let's recap next steps...
13:50 Samir (Redwood): Recap: Redwood lab run (Emily/Jordan), Zenith to provide topology, prompts and proxy logs, meet again after lab to review results.
14:02 Alex (Zenith): Thanks all.
14:06 Priya (Zenith): Appreciate the practical notes.
14:10 Samir (Redwood): We'll send meeting notes and the action item list. Thanks everyone.
